action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name

- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Perform CRUD operations on Directus Collections.

<actions>

- `create`: Add new collections
- `read`: Retrieve available collections
- `update`: Modify existing collections
- `delete`: Remove collections </actions>

<collection_structure>

### Collection Structure

```json
{
	"collection": "products",
	"meta": {
		"collection": "products",
		"icon": "inventory_2", // Any Material Symbols icons
		"note": "Main product catalog with inventory tracking", // Helpful 1 sentence description
		"color": "#6366F1", // Color shown in content module sidebar
		"singleton": false, // Single-item collections (settings, globals)
		"hidden": false, // Hide from navigation
		"accountability": "all", // Track who activity and revisions (`"all"`, `"activity"`, `null`)
		"sort_field": "sort", // Default sorting field (auto-creates if needed)
		"archive_app_filter": true, // Enable soft delete in the app
		"archive_field": "status", // Field used for archiving (status, deleted_at, etc.)
		"archive_value": "archived", // Value that marks items as archived
		"unarchive_value": "published", // Value that marks items as active
		"display_template": "{{name}} - ${{price}}",
		"versioning": false, // Enable content versioning for this collection
		"sort": 2, // Sort order for this collection
		"group": null, // Parent collection (use to group and nest collections in data model)
		"collapse": "open", // Default collection to expanded or collapsed if child collections
		"preview_url": "https://store.example.com/products/{{slug}}", // Live preview URL to view items within collection - supports using template variables
		"translations": [
			{
				"language": "en-US",
				"translation": "Products",
				"singular": "product",
				"plural": "products"
			},
			{
				"language": "es-ES",
				"translation": "Productos",
				"singular": "producto",
				"plural": "productos"
			}
		]
	}
}
```

**409 unique campers** had at least one confirmed week in the 2026 Summer Sailing Camps.

| Waitlisted only, never confirmed | 52 |

| **Total with an active registration** | 474 |

If some of them actually attended, the true number is between 409 and 422.

# Capture an Issue

Turn a problem — from the current conversation or the user's description — into a well-formed GitHub issue in `cyc-seattle/isthmia`.

## When to file one

File an issue when the work will outlive the current session: a problem found mid-task that you
are deliberately not fixing now, a known defect with no owner, or work that needs to be scheduled.

Do **not** file an issue for work you are about to do in this session. The session's pull request
records it. See the Workflow section of `CLAUDE.md`.

## Steps

1. **Gather the problem.** Pull details from the conversation or ask the user. A good issue needs: what's wrong or wanted, where in the code (`path:line`), and why it matters.
2. **Check for duplicates first.** `gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,title,labels`. If it overlaps an existing issue, tell the user and offer to comment on / rescope that one instead of filing a new duplicate.
3. **Pick a type label:** `bug`, `enhancement`, `documentation`, or `docker`.
4. **Assign a priority label** using the rubric below.
5. **Write the body** using the template below. Reference concrete files as `path:line`.
6. **Create it:** `gh issue create --title "<imperative title>" --label "<type>,<priority>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"`
7. **Report** the issue number and URL back to the user.

## Priority rubric (P0–P3)

- **P0 — Critical:** data integrity/corruption, production broken, or a security-critical hole. Work starts immediately.
- **P1 — High:** a significant bug or friction the user hits regularly, with no safe workaround (e.g. auth/tooling breakage).
- **P2 — Medium:** a real improvement or a bug with a workaround (added tests, hardening, moderate bugs).
- **P3 — Low:** cleanup, docs, polish, low-risk nice-to-haves.

## Body template

Keep it tight. Use `## Problem` always; then `## Fix` (bugs) or `## Proposed changes` / `## Scope` (enhancements); add `## Impact` when the "why" isn't obvious.

```markdown
## Problem

<what's wrong/wanted, with `path:line` references and a code snippet if useful>

## Fix

<concrete change; mention adding a regression test for bugs>

## Impact

<why it matters — omit if self-evident>
```

## Conventions

- **Title:** short, imperative, no priority prefix (priority lives in the label). e.g. "safeCall retries non-retryable errors with a 60s delay".
- Labels already exist: `P0`–`P3`, `bug`, `enhancement`, `documentation`, `docker`. Don't invent new ones without asking.
- For bugs, always note that the fix should include a regression test — tests live in `packages/*/test/**/*.test.ts`.
- Cross-link related issues with `#N` and note dependencies ("land #47 first").

Auth info does not live on `people`. Directus already has its own identity table — `directus_users`
— with roles, policies, and OIDC `provider`/`external_identifier` fields for linking a Google login.
Reusing it instead of a homegrown field means:

- `people.directus_user_id` is a nullable, unique FK to `directus_users.id`, declared in
  `packages/directus`'s schema — Directus is itself a provider, so its own identity column is an
  extension field on `people` like any other. Set only for people who have an actual login: staff
  now (provisioned directly by an admin); coach/guardian later, once #65's account-linking flow
  provisions or links a `directus_users` row on first OIDC login.
- Directus's own OIDC config does the email-matching (`provider` + `external_identifier` on
  `directus_users`). This schema has no identity/matching logic of its own — it only points `people`
  at the resulting user once one exists.

### Permission model

- **Administrator** — Directus's built-in full-access role.
- **Staff** — authenticates via Directus's native Google OIDC, restricted to Workspace accounts an
  admin has provisioned as Directus users. Full read/write on every collection above, including
  `medical_profiles`. The only role delivered end-to-end by #69/#92-#95.
- **Coach** — defined now so the schema doesn't need reshaping later, but has no way to log in yet
  (needs #65). KISS for now: any authenticated Directus user can read `sessions` /
  `registration_entries` / `people` roster fields (no `medical_profiles`) — scoping a coach to only
  their own sessions via `event_staff` is a follow-up, not built here.
- **Guardian** — same login caveat as Coach. Policy: read their own minors' `people` /
  `medical_profiles` / `registrations` / `registration_entries`, filtered through `contacts` where
  `relationship_type == 'guardian'`. This scoping isn't KISS'd away like the coach roster case above
  — it's the medical-data boundary the permission model exists to get right. Collection-level
  permissions are what's built; whether `medical_profiles` needs field-level restrictions too is a
  question for whenever a Guardian actually logs in (#65), not settled here.
- **Emergency contacts get no role or login.** They're informational rows staff can see on a minor's
  record (`contacts` where `relationship_type == 'emergency_contact'`), not a portal audience.
## Problem

The portal (`packages/portal/src/links.ts`) already groups links into audience sections ("Everyone", "Staff", "Volunteers", "Instructors"), but `renderPage` in `packages/portal/src/render.ts:32-33` renders every section for every viewer — the grouping is cosmetic, not access control. Anyone who passes the site-wide oauth2-proxy gate (all@ group, see `packages/infrastructure/src/portal.ts:9`) sees all sections, including any admin-only links added to them (e.g. Pulumi, Directus).

The portal was deliberately built as a static site with no app backend (#82) — a single pre-rendered HTML page — so there's currently no per-viewer identity available at render time to filter on.

## Proposed changes

Needs a design decision before implementation, since the options trade off the "no backend" constraint from #82:

1. **Client-side filtering** — ship all sections in the HTML/JS, but hide non-matching ones in the browser based on the viewer's identity (e.g. call oauth2-proxy's userinfo endpoint or a Google group-membership check client-side). Keeps the static-hosting model but the links are still present in page source for anyone who inspects it, and needs the group-membership plumbing noted in the caveats of the Google group-membership work.
2. **Dynamic render at request time** — have Caddy/oauth2-proxy forward the authenticated email (and resolved role/group) as a header to a small render step, and generate the page per-request. This is a real backend, reversing the #82 decision.
3. **Build-time per-role pages** — pre-render one static page per role (e.g. `/staff`, `/it-admin`) and rely on the network path (Caddy routing, or separate oauth2-proxy group checks per path) to gate which one a viewer can reach. Avoids a runtime backend but needs a role→path mapping and either multiple oauth2-proxy configs or group-aware routing.

Whichever approach is chosen, add an explicit `roles`/`audience` field to `Link`/`Section` in `packages/portal/src/links.ts` (the audience grouping already doubles as a natural role key) and cover the filtering logic with a unit test in `packages/portal/test/`.

## Impact

Right now any admin-only link (Pulumi console, Directus admin) added to the portal is visible to every CYC staff member/volunteer who can reach cycsail.team, not just IT admins. Low severity today since Pulumi/Directus have their own auth, but it's the wrong shape for an admin/reports link that shouldn't be casually discoverable.

Race team families have no way to find the other people on their team. Carpools, regatta travel, and school-team coordination all need a roster. The roster should cover the whole team at the program level, such as "Double-handed Race Team" (`programs`), not a single class like J-Pod.

The CRM already holds the data: `people.school`, guardian `contacts`, and registrations joined through `classes.program_id` to `programs`. But the guardian policy in `packages/infrastructure/src/crm/index.ts:104` only lets a guardian read their own minors, and it is read-only. Guardians and participants also have no login yet (#65).

## Proposed changes

- A roster view per program and season. It lists every participant with a confirmed entry in any class that maps to the program, along with each participant's school and guardian contact info.
- A school view. It lists the people on the same team who attend the same school.
- Guardians and participants can log in, then see and update their own data (the guardian for their minors).
- A roster-scoped read permission that exposes contact fields only to people on the same program. It never exposes `medical_profiles`.

Needs a design first. Open questions:

- Where does the roster UI live? Options are the Directus app, a portal page (#98), or something else.
- Does a participant get their own login, or only guardians?
- Do families need to opt in before their contact info is shared?
- Clubspot is the source of truth for these fields. How do edits flow back so the next sync (#137) doesn't overwrite them?

Depends on #65 (guardian login). Related to #156 (roles as groups) and #69.
EOF
)"

content.text:
You won't be working on #166 yet, so here are the options for planning. One thing shapes all of them: the only identity you have for a family is the email address they gave Clubspot. Whatever login you pick has to prove the person owns that email, then match it to a row in `people` or `contacts`. The options differ mainly in how well they cover families who don't use Gmail.

## Login options

**1. "Sign in with Google" (recommended as the main path).** Directus already logs staff in with Google (see the Caddyfile). You'd open that same Google login to any Google account and match on email. On first login, anyone whose email isn't a guardian or participant in the CRM gets no access.
- **Pros:** Nothing new to run, and most families already have a Google account.
- **Cons:** It fails when the Clubspot email isn't a Google account, such as Outlook, Yahoo, or work addresses. The Google OAuth client probably has to change from "Internal" to "External" before non-Workspace accounts can sign in. With only basic email and profile scopes, that doesn't need Google's review.

**2. Emailed sign-in link or one-time code (recommended as the fallback).** The family types their email, gets a link or code, and they're in. This works for every email address in Clubspot, and there's no password.
- **Cons:** Directus has no built-in email sign-in. You'd build a small Directus extension that sends the code and starts a session, or run a separate login service (next option). You'd also need a way to send email; the SES plan in #71 would cover it.

**3. A login service in front of everything (Authentik, Zitadel, or Keycloak).** One service offers Google, Microsoft, and emailed codes, then passes the result to Directus and oauth2-proxy.
- **Pros:** It covers the most families with no custom login code.
- **Cons:** It's another stateful service on the VM that has to be backed up, patched, and secured. It's probably too heavy until more than one app needs it.

**4. Add Microsoft and Apple sign-in to Directus.** Directus supports several login providers at once, so this could sit next to Google. Microsoft is easy. Apple is fiddly: it needs a paid developer account, and it can hide the user's real email, which breaks email matching.

**5. Sign in with Clubspot. Rejected.** Clubspot doesn't offer third-party login. Faking it would mean taking families' Clubspot passwords and replaying them against Parse, which is fragile and a security problem.

## Where the UI could live

- **The Directus app itself.** It works on day one with scoped permissions, but it's an admin tool: confusing for parents and poor on phones. It's fine for a pilot, not the end state.
- **A small web app that uses Directus as its backend (recommended).** A phone-friendly single page on the VM that calls Directus's API with the family's own login. Directus permissions stay the security boundary, and the app is just display and edit forms. `docs/crm-schema.md` already expects this ("thin clients calling this API").
- **Extending the portal.** The portal is a static page gated to the `all@` group (#82, #98). Opening it to families would mean reversing both decisions, so a separate app is cleaner.

## My recommendation

- Use Google sign-in through Directus's existing login as the main path.
- Add an emailed sign-in code as the fallback for non-Google emails.
- Put a small phone-friendly roster app in front of Directus.
- Run a short pilot with one team in the Directus app itself to settle what fields families actually want before building UI.
- Delay a separate login service until a second app needs families to log in.

Before choosing, it's worth checking one number: what share of race team guardian emails are Gmail or Google Workspace addresses. I can pull it from the CRM. If it's 90% or more, the emailed-code fallback could come later.

When you're ready, I can run the `design` skill to turn this into a design doc in `.claude/plans/` for you to approve.

message.content: Okay, I think I want to support login with Google as the main flow, with an email code as backup. What about using Google Workspace directly as the email provider - this might not scale, but I can get by for now before spinning up some other provider. I think we build this as an extension to the portal - the idea of the portal is specifically that it's for all the CYC Community: participants, staff, volunteers, etc... The app should be accessible to participants and guardians, contact sharing should be opt-in. For the next season (Spring), I can make that a custom field in clubspot so people can opt-in when the register. I don't think I need edits: read-only is good for now (except for the opt-in). Now, give me the pros and cons of using Authentik vs... something custom.

content.thinking:
I should weigh Authentik against a custom auth solution, keeping it brief. On the email side, Gmail sending limits matter — Workspace seats allow 2,000/day, SMTP relay 10,000/day via API — which is plenty; this fits with the earlier plan to use one Workspace seat for FreeScout, either directly or through a group alias as a sendAs address. I also want to flag that the portal is currently static, which has implications for extending it later.

The bigger point is that Authentik could replace oauth2-proxy's IdP role entirely, either by feeding it as an OIDC provider or by using Authentik's own forward-auth outpost with Caddy — a real advantage since the portal serves the whole community and a unified login could cover Directus, FreeScout, and Listmonk too. Authentik can source Google as a social login and, through its flow builder, support email-link or OTP-style verification flows, though I should hedge slightly since built-in email MFA support depends on version. Resource-wise, Authentik needs Postgres, which Cloud SQL can provide.

On the alternative, building custom email OTP and Google OIDC directly into Directus would avoid adding a new service and stay within the existing stack, but it means writing security-sensitive code — rate limiting, code expiry, brute-force protection — and there's no clean public API to mint a Directus session from an extension, which is a real blocker for that approach.

Given the goal of one identity layer across the portal, Directus, and future tools like FreeScout and Listmonk, I lean toward recommending Authentik, since it centralizes the email OTP risk instead of making us maintain it, at the cost of one extra service to run. Community roles like participant or guardian could then be mapped from Authentik group membership.

On email delivery: Workspace SMTP relay (smtp-relay.gmail.com) with IP-allowlisting from the VM's static IP is the cleaner fit for Authentik's SMTP needs, supporting up to 10k/day without needing app passwords, whereas a custom solution could instead use the Gmail API with domain-wide delegation.

For the Clubspot opt-in field, it'll land in custom_field_responses, and the existing promoted_fields mechanism already maps custom fields to people columns — worth a brief mention since that infrastructure exists. I should avoid asking questions in the response and just close with a clear recommendation.

content.text:
Workspace can handle the sign-in code emails fine at your size. Send them through Google's SMTP relay (`smtp-relay.gmail.com`), which you set up in the Workspace admin console. The relay can allow mail from the VM's static IP, so you don't need an app password, and the limit is about 10,000 recipients a day. Sending as a single mailbox allows about 2,000 a day. Either way, a few hundred families is far below the limit, and moving to SES later only means changing the SMTP settings.

## Authentik

**Pros**
- **One login for the whole community.** Authentik becomes the single identity provider, and Directus, the portal, and later FreeScout and Listmonk all trust it. That fits your "portal for everyone" idea: one "Sign in with Google or get a code" screen for staff, volunteers, participants, and guardians. It can also replace oauth2-proxy, because Authentik has its own proxy that Caddy can check requests against.
- **You don't write the risky code.** Short-lived codes, rate limits, brute-force lockout, session expiry, and logout are the easy parts to get subtly wrong. Authentik has had security audits.
- **Setup instead of code.** Google sign-in and an emailed code or link are both assembled in Authentik's visual flow editor from built-in steps. The trade-off is that flows are configured by clicking, so they need exporting as blueprints to live in the repo.
- **Better login screens** than Directus's: branding, a "check your email" page, and account recovery.

**Cons**
- **Another service with state.** It needs its own Postgres database, which can live on the existing Cloud SQL instance, and roughly 1–2 GB of RAM for its server and background worker. Check that the VM has headroom. It also needs backups (#66) and regular upgrades, and if Authentik is down, nobody can log in anywhere.
- **Some of its config lives outside the repo.** Flows and providers are managed in its UI unless you keep them as blueprints, which cuts against your infrastructure-as-code pattern. There's a Terraform provider, and Pulumi can bridge to it, but that's more setup.
- **It only says who someone is.** It doesn't know who is a guardian of whom. That still comes from the CRM, and Directus permissions still decide what each person sees. So you'd have two places to reason about access: Authentik for login, Directus for data.
- **Several logins to connect.** Authentik has to trust Google, and then Directus and the portal each have to trust Authentik. That's three connections to debug the first time.

## Custom (Directus handles login)

In this version, Directus's existing Google login is the main path, and a Directus extension you write sends the emailed codes. The portal becomes an app that signs people in through Directus and shows sections based on their Directus role, and oauth2-proxy is retired from the portal.

**Pros**
- **Nothing new to run.** It stays within the Directus-plus-Caddy setup you already have, with no new database, backups, or upgrades.
- **One place decides access.** Identity and data permissions both live in Directus. The same role that lets someone read the roster also decides which portal sections they see, which also solves #98 for free.
- **All of it is code in the repo,** tested and reviewed like everything else.

**Cons**
- **You own security-sensitive code:** code generation, expiry, attempt limits, protection against guessing which emails exist, and rate limiting. It's small, but a bug here exposes minors' contact info.
- **Directus has no supported way to start a session for someone who proved their email.** Directus sessions start from a password or a login provider. An extension would have to mint tokens itself or reach into Directus internals, which is fragile across Directus upgrades.
- **Everything depends on Directus.** Any future app that needs family login, such as FreeScout, would need Directus to act as a login provider for other apps, which it can't do. You'd end up adding Authentik anyway, with a migration on top.
- **Every page family members see sits on Directus.** That's fine for a read-only roster, but it ties the portal's availability to the CRM's.

## Recommendation

Go with Authentik. The case for building it yourself was "one small app," but making the portal the front door for the whole community changes that. You're really choosing the identity layer for every future app, and the one custom piece you'd write, emailed-code login, is the part I'd least want to own for a site holding minors' data. The cost is running one more service, which your Cloud SQL, Caddy, and Pulumi setup already supports.

The main thing to confirm before committing is whether the VM has 1–2 GB of spare memory. Without it, Authentik also means a bigger VM, which moves the monthly cost.

Your Clubspot opt-in custom field will sync into `custom_field_responses`, and the existing `promoted_fields` mechanism can copy it onto a `people` column. The roster permission can then filter on that column.

content.text:
Mostly it shouldn't. Let Authentik answer "who is this?" and let Directus answer "what can they see?" Directus's permission rules can already filter rows based on the signed-in user, and the guardian rules use this today. The filter in `packages/infrastructure/src/crm/index.ts:93` walks from a record to `contacts` to the signed-in user (`directus_user_id = $CURRENT_USER`). A roster rule would work the same way.

## How a request flows

1. **Login.** The portal sends the family member to Authentik, where they sign in with Google or an emailed code. Authentik returns a verified email address.
2. **Directus account.** Directus trusts Authentik as a login provider. On first login it creates a Directus user automatically, with a family role that grants nothing on its own.
3. **Match to the CRM.** The new Directus user is linked to its `people` row by email, which sets `people.directus_user_id`. The linking can be a Directus hook that runs when a user is created, or a step in the sync job. If no email matches, the link never happens, and every rule that depends on it matches nothing. So someone whose email isn't in the CRM sees an empty app.
4. **Data.** The portal page calls Directus's API with that user's session. The roster rule says, in effect: show people with a confirmed entry in a program where I, or a child I'm a guardian of, also have a confirmed entry, and who have opted in. Directus applies it on every query, so the portal never makes a permission decision about data.

Step 4 has one practical wrinkle. The portal is on `cycsail.team` and Directus is on its own `directus.*` hostname. If that's a subdomain of `cycsail.team`, the browser treats both as the same site, and Directus's session cookie works for API calls from the portal. If it's a separate domain, the portal needs a token exchange or a same-origin proxy route through Caddy. The design doc should settle this.

## Where Authentik does need CRM data

Authentik needs CRM data for one decision: which portal sections someone can see, such as staff, volunteers, or families. That's a group membership. There are three ways to get it into Authentik:

- **A sync job pushes CRM roles into Authentik groups (recommended).** It would be a new provider package with the same plan-and-execute shape as `gsuite-sync`, reading `program_roles` and registrations and writing Authentik groups through its API. This is the "model roles once, map them into each product" idea from #156, with Authentik as one more product. Authentik then includes the groups in its login token, and the portal and Caddy gate on them.
- **Authentik calls Directus when someone logs in.** Authentik's login steps can run Python code, so one could query Directus and assign groups on the fly. It's always current, but it's logic hidden in Authentik's config instead of tested code, and if Directus is down, nobody can log in.
- **Skip groups and let Directus decide.** The portal asks Directus "what's my role?" after login and shows sections to match. It's the simplest option, but then Authentik only guards entry to the site, not individual sections.

## Recommendation

Use Directus permissions for all data access, and the sync job for Authentik groups. The only thing Authentik learns from the CRM is coarse group membership, which gates what's shown. The rules that protect contact data stay in the Pulumi-managed permission rules and can be tested. And if someone's groups are an hour stale, they only see the wrong portal sections; they never get data Directus wouldn't give them.

## FreeScout OAuth/OIDC Support

FreeScout has an OAuth & Social Login Module, and FreeScout now supports OIDC through a purchasable module at https://freescout.net/module/oauth-login. There is also a community OAuth module for FreeScout that was tested with Keycloak OAuth provider with confidential OpenID-connect client.

Additionally, FreeScout offers a SAML 2.0 SSO Module that enables single sign-on authentication for users, where FreeScout works as a Service Provider (SP) and allows users from an Identity Provider (IdP) to authenticate in FreeScout.

## Authentik as an Identity Provider

Authentik can be implemented for Single Sign-On (SSO) by deploying it as a centralized identity provider and configuring OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication. Authentik is an open-source identity provider that centralizes authentication with support for OAuth2/OIDC, SAML, LDAP, and proxy authentication.

## Integration Potential

While the search results show that both FreeScout and Authentik support OIDC/OAuth protocols, there isn't specific documentation about integrating FreeScout with Authentik in these results. However, FreeScout's OAuth module should theoretically be compatible with Authentik since both support standard OIDC protocols.

content.content:
# FreeScout OAuth Module and Generic OIDC Providers

Based on the forum discussion, the FreeScout OAuth module **does appear to support custom OIDC providers**. A user reports: "We use the FreeScout OAuth module connected to Google, and we do not use LDAP."

However, there's a critical issue: when using Cloudron's user management integration, the system auto-configures OIDC settings and overwrites custom configurations on restart. A staff member explains the problem: "Because of this, it takes ownership of the OIDC provider settings and reconfigures the OIDC provider."

**The workaround** is to install FreeScout with the option "Let the app manage it's own users" rather than using Cloudron user management, which prevents the autoconfiguration from interfering with custom OIDC provider settings.

The forum doesn't explicitly detail whether the module supports custom authorize/token/userinfo URLs, but the ability to configure Google OAuth suggests it supports external OIDC providers beyond the auto-configured Cloudron integration.

# OAuth FreeScout Module Analysis

## Configuration Requirements

The module accepts three OAuth endpoint URLs:

1. **Authorization Endpoint URL** - for initiating login
2. **Token Endpoint URL** - for exchanging authorization codes
3. **User Info Endpoint URL** - for retrieving user details

Plus standard OAuth credentials: Client ID and Client Secret.

## Maintenance Status

The repository shows **11 total commits** on the master branch, but **no last commit date is displayed** in the provided content. This makes it impossible to determine if the project is actively maintained.

## Provider Compatibility

The documentation includes **Azure Active Directory (AAD)** configuration details. The module was also "tested on keycloak oauth provider with confidential openid-connect client."

## User Auto-Creation

**No auto-creation** - the documentation explicitly states: "User must be registered before oauth login." Users require pre-existing accounts to authenticate via OAuth.

## Additional Notes

- Requires PHP curl extension
- Replaces standard login with OAuth redirection
- Allows bypassing OAuth with `?disable_oauth=1` parameter

content.text:
Yes, FreeScout can log in through Authentik using its paid SAML module. The OAuth module will probably work too, but I couldn't confirm that from the docs.

- **SAML SSO module (confirmed).** FreeScout's page says it works with "any SAML 2.0 Identity Provider," and Authentik can act as one. It can also create a FreeScout user automatically on first login, filling in name, job title, and phone from the login. Authentik isn't one of its worked examples, which are Auth0, JumpCloud, Azure, and Google Workspace, but that doesn't limit which providers it supports.
- **OAuth & Social Login module (likely, not confirmed).** It ships preset setups for Google, Azure, GitHub, and Auth0. Its Azure notes mention editing an "Authorization URL," which suggests the endpoint addresses can be changed and pointed at Authentik. Neither the page nor Authentik's integration list confirms it works with Authentik.
- **Free community OAuth module (not recommended).** [fhirter-vkb/freescout-oauth](https://github.com/fhirter-vkb/freescout-oauth) takes the three standard login addresses and was tested against Keycloak, so it would work with Authentik. But it can't create users on first login, and it has only 11 commits with no sign of recent upkeep.

Two things limit how much Authentik would give you in FreeScout:

1. **Neither paid module assigns users to mailboxes or teams.** Both pages say so. Authentik groups can't decide who sees which inbox, so you'd still set that by hand in FreeScout. That cuts against the "model roles once" plan in #156 for this one app.
2. **Few people would use it.** Under the mailbox decision from August, outside assignees reply to notification emails and never log in. Only staff would use single sign-on in FreeScout, and they already have Google accounts. So FreeScout alone doesn't justify Authentik: its SAML module could trust Google Workspace directly. Authentik is still justified by the portal and the family logins.

If you go with Authentik, use the SAML module for FreeScout. It's the only option confirmed to work with any login provider. Either paid module is a one-time license per FreeScout instance; neither page showed a price.

- [SAML SSO Module – FreeScout](https://freescout.net/module/saml/)
- [OAuth & Social Login Module – FreeScout](https://freescout.net/module/oauth-login/)
- [fhirter-vkb/freescout-oauth](https://github.com/fhirter-vkb/freescout-oauth)
- [FreeScout OIDC Support – Cloudron Forum](https://forum.cloudron.io/topic/13260/freescout-oidc-support)
- [Integrations overview – authentik](https://integrations.goauthentik.io/)

message.content: I'm trying to see how authentik, directus, and oauth-proxy fit together here. can you give me a simple diagram and explain

content.thinking:
I'm sketching a simple terminal diagram to reason through the architecture. With Authentik in place, I'm considering whether oauth2-proxy becomes redundant since Authentik's proxy outpost can handle forward auth directly, or whether it's better to keep oauth2-proxy but point it at Authentik as the OIDC provider—leaning toward replacing it with the embedded outpost. I'm also questioning whether the portal even needs forward-auth given it's a static page with gated sections that calls Directus.

Sketching the diagram flow...

Then I want to explain oauth2-proxy's current role as Google-based gatekeeper with an all@ email check, and recommend removing it in favor of Authentik's forward_auth outpost, since keeping it around adds unnecessary complexity — a small before/after diagram pair should make that clear.

content.text:
Here's today's setup next to the proposed one.

**Today**

```
Browser ──► Caddy ─┬─ cycsail.team ──► oauth2-proxy ──► Google (must be in all@) ──► Portal (static page)
                   │
                   └─ directus.* ───► Directus ──► Google (its own login) ──► Postgres (CRM)
```

Two separate gatekeepers each talk to Google on their own. oauth2-proxy guards the portal, and Directus guards itself.

**Proposed**

```
                        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                        │ Authentik                    │
                        │ "who are you?"               │
                        │ • Sign in with Google        │
                        │ • or emailed code            │
                        │ • knows your groups          │
                        └──────▲───────────────▲───────┘
            "logged in? which  │               │ "log me in" (OIDC)
             groups?"          │               │
Browser ──► Caddy ─┬─ cycsail.team ──► Portal page ──── API calls ────► Directus ──► Postgres
                   │                  (shows sections                  "what can you see?"
                   │                   by group)                        (row-level rules)
                   └─ directus.* ──────────────────────────────────────► Directus
                                                                            ▲
                                        sync job: reads CRM roles ──────────┘
                                        and writes Authentik groups
```

## What each piece does

- **Caddy** is the front door. It handles TLS and routes by hostname, as it does today.
- **Authentik** answers one question: who is this person? It's the only thing that talks to Google or sends codes. It also carries coarse groups, such as staff, volunteer, or race team family, which a sync job copies in from the CRM.
- **The portal** is the page people see. It asks Authentik which groups the viewer is in and shows the matching sections. The roster section fetches its data from Directus.
- **Directus** answers the other question: what can this person see? It trusts Authentik's login instead of talking to Google itself. Its permission rules filter every query down to the viewer's own team, opted-in families only, and no medical data. The portal never decides who sees which rows.

## Where oauth2-proxy goes

oauth2-proxy goes away. Its whole job today is asking Caddy "is this request logged in, and are they in all@?" Authentik has a built-in proxy that answers the same question for Caddy, using Authentik's own groups. Keeping oauth2-proxy would put two gatekeepers in a row: Caddy asks oauth2-proxy, which asks Authentik.

You could keep oauth2-proxy and point it at Authentik instead of Google, which is a smaller change to the Caddyfile. It still adds nothing Authentik can't do, so I'd plan to remove it.

## One login, end to end

1. A parent opens `cycsail.team`. Caddy asks Authentik whether they're logged in. They aren't, so Authentik shows "Sign in with Google" or "Email me a code."
2. They sign in. Authentik now knows their email and groups, for example "race team family," and the portal shows the roster section.
3. The roster section calls Directus. Directus sees the same Authentik login, matches it to the parent's `people` row, and returns only their team's opted-in contacts.

The layers split cleanly: Authentik and its groups decide what someone can reach, and Directus decides what data they get. If a group is wrong, someone sees the wrong menu, but Directus still hands them only their own team's opted-in contacts.

content.content:
## Problem

Race team families have no way to find the other people on their team. Carpools, regatta travel, and school-team coordination all need a roster. The roster should cover the whole team at the program level, such as "Double-handed Race Team" (`programs`), not a single class like J-Pod.

The CRM already holds the data: `people.school`, guardian `contacts`, and registrations joined through `classes.program_id` to `programs`. But the guardian policy in `packages/infrastructure/src/crm/index.ts:104` only lets a guardian read their own minors, and it is read-only. Guardians and participants also have no login yet (#65).

## Proposed changes

- A roster view per program and season. It lists every participant with a confirmed entry in any class that maps to the program, along with each participant's school and guardian contact info.
- A school view. It lists the people on the same team who attend the same school.
- Guardians and participants can log in, then see and update their own data (the guardian for their minors).
- A roster-scoped read permission that exposes contact fields only to people on the same program. It never exposes `medical_profiles`.

Needs a design first. Open questions:

- Where does the roster UI live? Options are the Directus app, a portal page (#98), or something else.
- Does a participant get their own login, or only guardians?
- Do families need to opt in before their contact info is shared?
- Clubspot is the source of truth for these fields. How do edits flow back so the next sync (#137) doesn't overwrite them?

Depends on #65 (guardian login). Related to #156 (roles as groups) and #69.

content.text:
I've recorded the Authentik decision in #166, along with the other choices from this conversation: Google sign-in first with an emailed code as backup, Workspace as the email sender, the roster as part of the portal, read-only apart from the opt-in, opt-in sharing, and the split between Authentik groups and Directus permissions. The issue also notes that this changes the approach in #65, which assumed oauth2-proxy with Google.

Here's what's still open. The first group needs you; the design doc can propose answers for the second.

## Decisions that need you

1. **Participant logins.** Can minors log in, and from what age? Many race team kids are under 13. Clubspot also often lists a parent's email on the child's record, so one email may belong to both a parent and a child.
2. **What the roster shows.** For example: participant name and school, guardian names, emails, and phones. The question is whether a minor's own phone or email ever appears.
3. **What opting in covers.** Is it per family or per person, and does it renew each season or stay until withdrawn?
4. **Fall, before the Clubspot field exists.** Either the roster starts empty and families opt in through the app, or it waits until Spring.
5. **Which programs and seasons count.** Only race team programs, or anything mapped to a program? Current season only? Should coaches appear on the roster?
6. **Sign-off on sharing minors' data.** Whether the board or your safeguarding policy needs to approve sharing minors' contact info before launch. That's a question for the org, not code.

## For the design doc to propose

- **Order of work.** Move the existing portal and staff onto Authentik first with no change in behavior, then add families. Or do both at once.
- **Where staff groups come from.** Google Groups (`all@`, as today) or the CRM, and how that fits the Authentik sync.
- **Hosting.** Memory headroom on the VM, and Authentik's database on the existing Cloud SQL instance.
- **Keeping config in the repo.** Authentik blueprints versus a Pulumi provider.
- **Hostnames.** The name for Authentik, and whether Directus shares a parent domain with the portal so its session works for the portal's API calls.
- **Email matching.** One email linked to several `people` rows, emails that change, and what someone with no match sees.
- **School names.** They're free text from Clubspot, so the school view may need them cleaned up and grouped.
- **Opt-in edits vs. sync.** A family changes their opt-in in the app, and the next Clubspot sync overwrites it. That's the #137 problem, and the design has to say which one wins.
- **Email sender.** Which Workspace address sends the codes, and checking that SPF and DKIM cover the relay.

Let me ask about the ones that shape the design most.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/skills/design

# Design a Change

Produce a short design doc, get it approved, and hand it to `implement`. No code is written until the user approves the doc.

Use this only for tier-3 work. Most tasks do not need a design doc. If the approach is obvious, skip straight to `implement`.

## 1. Dispatch the designer

Use `Agent` with `subagent_type: designer`.

The agent knows the doc template, the investigation questions, and the repo pitfalls — they are in `.claude/agents/designer.md`. The prompt carries only:

- The problem, in the user's own words where possible.
- Any constraint or preference the user has already stated.
- Anything already ruled out, and why.

The agent writes the doc to `.claude/plans/` and reports its path, a summary, and its open questions. It cannot edit source files.

Stay available while it works. This is the longest sub-agent dispatch in the workflow.

## 2. Read it yourself

Read the doc before you show it to the user. You are accountable for what you put in front of them.

Check that it cites real code, that the steps are genuinely separable, and that the open questions are real decisions rather than research the agent skipped. Send it back if not.

## 3. Get approval

Show the user the doc path and a three-line summary. Ask directly for approval.

Answer their questions and edit the doc until they approve it. Do not start implementing while questions are open.

The user approves in conversation. There is no label and no PR gate for this.

## 4. Hand off

Once approved:

1. Commit the design doc on the session branch.
2. Run `implement` once per step in the Steps list.
3. If a step reveals the design was wrong, stop. Update the doc, tell the user what changed, and get agreement before continuing.

## Should this be a GitHub issue?

File one with `capture` only if the work will outlive this session. A design doc plus a same-session PR needs no issue.

If you do file one, link the design doc path from the issue body.

---
name: start-session
description: Open a work session — create the session branch, then triage each request the user makes into one of three tiers and dispatch it. Stays responsive between tasks. Use when the user starts a work session, says "let's work on some things", or begins a batch of changes meant to land as one PR.
---

# Start a Session

Entry point for the isthmia workflow. A **session** is one git worktree, one branch, one batch of work, and one pull request at the end.

Your job is to orchestrate, not to disappear into a task. The user treats this session like a browser main thread. Keep it free.

## Companion skills

Each step of the workflow is its own skill. Call them, do not re-implement them.

| Skill               | When                                            |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `capture`           | File a GitHub issue                             |
| `triage`            | Clean up the issue backlog                      |
| `design`            | Tier 3 — write a design doc and get it approved |
| `implement`         | Tier 2 and 3 — brief and dispatch a sub-agent   |
| `review`            | Review the session diff                         |
| `end-session`       | Verify, review, and open the PR                 |
| `technical-writing` | Any prose you write                             |

## 1. Open the session

Every session runs in its own **git worktree**. The user runs sessions in parallel in separate terminals, and a worktree is what keeps them from fighting over one working tree.

Do this once, at the start.

1. **Check where you are.** Run `git status --short` and `git branch --show-current`.
   - Already in a session worktree — use it. Do not nest worktrees.
   - The tree is dirty with unrelated changes — ask the user what to do first.
   - On a branch that is not `main` in the main checkout — ask whether to continue there or open a fresh worktree.

2. **Pick a name.** Propose a short slug for the work, such as `roster-reports` or `auth-cleanup`. Fall back to `session-YYYY-MM-DD` when the session has no theme yet. Confirm it with the user.

3. **Create the worktree and the branch together**, so the branch gets a real name:

   ```sh
   git fetch origin
   git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<slug> -b session/<slug> origin/main
   ```

   Then enter it with `EnterWorktree`, passing `path: .claude/worktrees/<slug>`.

   Creating the worktree with `EnterWorktree`'s `name` argument also works, but it names the branch `worktree-<slug>`, which reads badly in the pull request.

4. **Set the worktree up** with `just worktree` — git hooks, then dependencies.

   A `SessionStart` hook runs this already, so usually there is nothing to do. Run it by hand if
   the hook did not fire, or if a commit fails with "No .pre-commit-config.yaml file was found".

5. **Start a task list** with `TodoWrite`. It becomes the PR body at the end of the session.

6. Tell the user the session is open and name the worktree path. They can now describe tasks one at a time.

Never repeat this step. One worktree and one branch per session.

entries.name: EnterWorktree
entries.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

name.description: Optional name for a new worktree. Each "/"-separated segment may contain only letters, digits, dots, underscores, and dashes; max 64 chars total. A random name is generated if not provided. Mutually exclusive with `path`.

path.description: Path to an existing worktree to switch into instead of creating a new one. Must appear in `git worktree list` for the current repo — or, on first entry from the launch directory, for a repo nested inside it (multi-repo workspace). Mutually exclusive with `name`.
